entities.name: Robert d'Ufford, 1st Earl of Suffolk
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Robert d'Ufford, 1st Earl of Suffolk, KG, emerged as a pivotal English peer and military commander during the tumultuous reign of Edward III, serving as a cornerstone of the English war effort in the early phases of the Hundred Years' War. Born into a prominent East Anglian family, his ascent was marked by unwavering loyalty and distinguished service to the crown. Created Earl of Suffolk in 1337, he solidified his family's position within the English aristocracy and played a crucial role in shaping the military and political landscape of 14th-century England.

Throughout his long career, Ufford was at the forefront of major military engagements, demonstrating tactical acumen and bravery. He campaigned extensively in Scotland, participating in the Battle of Halidon Hill in 1333, and later became a key figure in the wars against France. His contributions included significant roles in the naval triumph at the Battle of Sluys in 1340, the innovative chevauchée of 1346 that culminated in the decisive English victory at the Battle of Crécy, and the subsequent Siege of Calais. These campaigns were instrumental in establishing England's early dominance in the Hundred Years' War and defining Edward III's aggressive foreign policy.

Ufford's legacy extends beyond military prowess; he was a statesman who served on numerous royal commissions and councils, influencing domestic policy and administration. His elevation to the earldom marked a significant consolidation of power for the Ufford family in Suffolk, a region vital for its agricultural wealth and strategic coastal access. As one of the original 26 Knights of the Garter, an order established around 1348, he became part of an elite chivalric fraternity that profoundly shaped the ideals of English knighthood and aristocratic identity for centuries.
